# A Vector Atlas curated resource for learning and levelling-up 

Vector Atlas is all about models. We make useful models that bring evidence to bear on vector control in countries with high malaria burden. Just as the utility of our models and map outputs about malaria vectors depend on well-placed assumptions, the utility of this resource was prepared according to our assumptions about your needs. Please let us know where we are off the mark. 

These pages are intended to help our PhD students, interns, career researchers and partners develop or dust-off sound research and working practices. 

Topics are grouped by the kind of practice they support, since we anticipate that most modules will be revisited at different points in a person's learning and practice.

Text will be minimal. Our intention is to give you a sense of the criteria behind the selection of the resources. Besides, some of these topics are moving _very_ fast indeed, and anything we write might be obsolete by the time we finish writing the sentence.

## 1. A working life in research

This fundamentally important element won't be the subject of much development here, since it is not our wheelhouse. That said, each person will benefit from developing some reflective habits and self-maintaining practices that can provide bedrock and orientation for your professional journey. Those kinds of practices can be particularly helpful when learning new skills or relearning skills that have proved hard to consolidate in your head, such as those we highlight in later sections.

- What is this?
- Defusing catastrophic thinking
- Seeking help
- Accepting good enough
- Looking after yourself (workload, isolation, identity-as-researcher)

## Threaded theme: using LLMs as a means to an end

Rather than addressing LLM use as a standalone module, it runs through the curriculum as applied practice. Each appearance should revisit a shared set of principles — prompting, verification, knowing when to trust output, attribution, reproducibility of LLM-assisted work — alongside the specific task.

Likely touchpoints:

- Literature engagement (2): summarising, finding related work, extracting conceptual structure
- Project management (3): drafting plans, outlines, progress notes
- Computing (4): code generation, debugging, refactoring, reproducible examples
- Quantitative reasoning (5): deriving, checking, and explaining maths
- Document preparation (7): drafting, editing, formatting
- Communication (8): tightening prose, generating variants, audience adaptation

## Cross-cutting topics

Some topics naturally reference multiple modules:

- **File management** underpins both project management (3) and computing (4).
- **Tailoring and exporting R plots** spans visualisation (6) and document preparation (7).
- **Your conceptual diagram** and **extracting someone else's conceptual model** are mirror skills (producing vs reading) bridging literature engagement (2) and visualisation (6).
- **Peer review** sits primarily with literature engagement (2) but cuts across collaboration (9) and paper-writing (8).
- **How to write a paper** draws on project management (3) as well as communication (8).

## Natural dependencies

Useful when sequencing sessions later:

- Reading and writing maths → writing a likelihood → point process models
- File management → writing reproducible code → git/GitHub → reproducible example
- Diagramming → your conceptual diagram → extracting others' conceptual models
- LaTeX or Quarto presupposes some comfort with plain-text tooling and git
